newsitem.title: USA: Eight of 12 Fed banks want discount rate up-source.
newsitem.headline: Eight of 12 Fed banks want discount rate up-source.

text.p: Eight of the 12 district banks in the Federal Reserve System have requested an increase in the five percent discount rate amid mounting evidence the pace of U.S. economic expansion is likely to remain brisk in the second half of 1996, a senior Fed official said on Tuesday.
"Eight (Fed) banks have requested a discount rate hike and (of those) three have requested a 50-basis-point discount rate hike," the source told Reuters.
The Fed Board discusses discount rate changes every Monday.
The remarks wiped out Wall Street's early gains on Tuesday. The market had previously largely believed rates would remain unchanged.
The Federal Open Market Committee next meets on September 24 when a rates decision may be taken.
That meeting could see the Fed board and the FOMC simultaneously announcing a 25-basis-point hike in both the discount rate and the 5.25-percent federal funds rate, the source said.
"There is a consensus (at the Fed) emerging around a 25-basis-point increase in the funds rate," the source added.

The source said the requests for a discount rate hike have been submitted by banks in Fed districts that are experiencing rapid growth and tight labor markets or that have a "hawkish" anti-inflation tradition.
The three district banks calling for a half-point discount rate hike are in Minneapolis, Richmond and San Francisco, according to the source.
"There has been a shift, recently, at the Fed," the source said, noting a widely expected second-half economic slowdown is not materialising as quickly as Fed economists predicted.

The source said the August employment report -- though its strength may have been exaggerated by special factors -- "gave the hawks fresh ammunition and raised questions about how far the (non-inflationary growth threshold) experiment can go."

The source added some of the Fed governors known for their moderate views on monetary policy -- such as Laurence Meyer -- were sympathetic to the bank presidents' concern that the U.S. economy may be overheating.

"We are not going to see another 4.0-percent-plus GDP (Gross Domestic Product growth) in the third quarter but it's likely to be still above trend," the source also said, predicting GDP "will be back to trend in 1997."
The Fed's last interest rate moves came on January 31, 1996, when the central bank lowered the discount and funds rates by 25 basis points each.
Those rate reductions came amid concern the U.S. expansion, after anaemic growth in the fourth quarter of 1995, was weakening.
That easing -- dubbed at the time an insurance policy -- is now regarded at the Fed as "a mistake," the source said.
The source also said the Fed is pleased with the absence of pressure in broad price measures -- but totally committed to not giving up any ground on the inflation front.

"Every measure of the wage component in labor costs points in the same direction. It's rising," the source added, noting the 5.1-percent August unemployment rate confirms anecdotal reports that U.S. labor markets have gotten very tight.
